Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript: Welcome to Module 8, Strings and Dates in PostgreSQL. Text and time values often look simple on the screen, but they carry important analytical meaning. In this module, we will clean text carefully, parse structured pieces from strings, use regular expressions when simple functions are not enough, choose appropriate date and time types, calculate intervals, group events by time grain, and work with time zones. Every SQL example can run directly in the browser, and you can copy the same query into pgAdmin for additional practice. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a CRM standardizing names, emails, and phone numbers. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Why this module matters
slides.transcript: This module is about more than display formatting. A trailing space can create a different category. Inconsistent case can fragment groups. A date stored as text cannot safely participate in date arithmetic. Time values also have different meanings. A calendar date is different from a local clock timestamp, and both are different from an instant stored with time-zone meaning. The goal is to prepare these values without accidentally changing what they mean. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a hospital calculating length of stay and follow-up dates. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript: By the end of the module, you should be able to normalize common text problems, choose the right temporal type, change time grain, calculate durations, and separate parsing from formatting. You should also be able to explain why a transformation is appropriate. The objective is not to memorize a long list of functions. It is to select the right function based on the meaning of the value and the analytical task. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, an operations team aligning timestamps across locations. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: PostgreSQL-specific correction
slides.transcript: One correction is important before we start. PostgreSQL does not use DATEADD and DATEDIFF as native functions. Instead, PostgreSQL commonly uses date or timestamp subtraction, INTERVAL values, EXTRACT, DATE_TRUNC, AGE, TO_DATE, TO_TIMESTAMP, and TO_CHAR. The underlying analytical ideas are portable, but the SQL syntax depends on the database system. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a CRM standardizing names, emails, and phone numbers, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Module roadmap
slides.transcript: The module has two main halves. First, we work with text: inspect, normalize, parse, and validate. Second, we work with time: choose the correct type, extract components, change analytical grain, calculate durations, and handle time zones. At the end, we combine the ideas in practical preparation tasks and projects. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a hospital calculating length of stay and follow-up dates. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Teaching database
slides.transcript: The teaching database combines healthcare-style and retail-style examples. Patients gives us messy contact text. Admissions gives us timestamps for elapsed-time calculations. Products helps with substring and replacement examples. Orders gives us timestamps and numeric measures for monthly summaries. Staging dates contains raw text dates in different formats so we can practice safe parsing. Connect this idea to an operations team aligning timestamps across locations. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Inspect raw text first
slides.transcript: The first step in text cleaning is inspection. Run this query and look closely at names, emails, and addresses. Do not decide on a cleaning rule before you understand the patterns that actually occur. Some values may have extra spaces, inconsistent capitalization, or abbreviations. The cleaning rule should respond to observed problems, not blindly transform every string. Connect this idea to a CRM standardizing names, emails, and phone numbers. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Text cleaning pipeline
slides.transcript: Text cleaning is a pipeline, not one magic function. First inspect the raw value. Then normalize only known formatting noise. If the string contains meaningful structure, parse the pieces you need. Validation is a separate step that asks whether the cleaned value follows an expected rule. Finally, use the cleaned field for analysis or reporting. When traceability matters, preserve the raw source value as well. Text cleaning should separate normalization from interpretation. Trimming spaces or standardizing case is usually safe when the rule is documented; correcting a person's name or guessing an email address is a much stronger intervention. Preserve the original value when auditability matters.

slides.title: Raw vs cleaned values
slides.transcript: A cleaned value should be explainable. In these examples, we remove formatting noise and apply a documented abbreviation rule. We are not inventing new information. Keeping raw and cleaned values side by side is useful during development because it makes every transformation visible. That helps catch over-cleaning and makes the process easier to audit. Connect this idea to an operations team aligning timestamps across locations. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Case functions
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL provides several case functions. UPPER makes all letters uppercase. LOWER makes all letters lowercase and is commonly useful for normalization before comparison. INITCAP capitalizes words for display. Be careful with names because real capitalization can be more complex than a simple function. A cleaning rule should fit the domain rather than assuming one display convention is universally correct. Text cleaning should separate normalization from interpretation. Trimming spaces or standardizing case is usually safe when the rule is documented; correcting a person's name or guessing an email address is a much stronger intervention. Preserve the original value when auditability matters.

slides.title: Case + trim + length
slides.transcript: Run this example to compare several functions at once. UPPER and LOWER change letter case. BTRIM removes spaces from the beginning and end. INITCAP creates a display-style name after trimming. LENGTH shows why invisible spaces matter: raw and trimmed strings can have different lengths even when they look similar on screen. Text cleaning should separate normalization from interpretation. Trimming spaces or standardizing case is usually safe when the rule is documented; correcting a person's name or guessing an email address is a much stronger intervention. Preserve the original value when auditability matters.

slides.title: BTRIM handles boundaries
slides.transcript: BTRIM is excellent for boundary whitespace. It removes spaces from the start and end of a string. But it does not collapse repeated spaces inside the value. That distinction is important. If you need to normalize internal whitespace, you need a different function such as REGEXP_REPLACE with a repeated-whitespace pattern. Text cleaning should separate normalization from interpretation. Trimming spaces or standardizing case is usually safe when the rule is documented; correcting a person's name or guessing an email address is a much stronger intervention. Preserve the original value when auditability matters.

slides.title: Why LENGTH is useful
slides.transcript: LENGTH is useful because text problems are not always visually obvious. Boundary spaces and repeated internal spaces increase the character count. Comparing length before and after cleaning can help confirm that your transformation is doing what you expect. Think of LENGTH as a diagnostic function during data preparation. Text cleaning should separate normalization from interpretation. Trimming spaces or standardizing case is usually safe when the rule is documented; correcting a person's name or guessing an email address is a much stronger intervention. Preserve the original value when auditability matters.

slides.title: Repeated whitespace
slides.transcript: Repeated internal whitespace requires a pattern-based solution. The PostgreSQL regular-expression pattern bracket colon space colon bracket represents whitespace. The plus means one or more occurrences. Replacing that run with one ordinary space turns values with inconsistent spacing into a more stable representation. We usually trim boundaries first and then normalize the internal whitespace. Text cleaning should separate normalization from interpretation. Trimming spaces or standardizing case is usually safe when the rule is documented; correcting a person's name or guessing an email address is a much stronger intervention. Preserve the original value when auditability matters.

slides.title: Normalize repeated spaces
slides.transcript: This query combines two cleaning steps. BTRIM removes boundary spaces. REGEXP_REPLACE then collapses repeated internal whitespace to one space. The g flag means replace every matching occurrence, not just the first. Run the query and compare the raw and normalized names row by row. Connect this idea to an operations team aligning timestamps across locations. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Combine fields carefully
slides.transcript: Sometimes the goal is to build one readable field from several columns. CONCAT_WS means concatenate with separator. It is especially useful when some components can be NULL because it avoids producing unnecessary separators for missing arguments. NULLIF can convert an empty string to NULL first. That combination helps create clean display lines without confusing blanks. Connect this idea to a CRM standardizing names, emails, and phone numbers. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Build a contact line
slides.transcript: This query creates one contact line. The name is trimmed and has repeated whitespace normalized. The email is trimmed, and NULLIF turns an empty string into NULL. The address is trimmed. CONCAT_WS joins the available pieces with a vertical-bar separator and skips NULL arguments. Run the query and inspect how missing values affect the output. In a real setting such as a hospital calculating length of stay and follow-up dates, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Structured strings can be parsed
slides.transcript: Some strings contain meaningful internal structure. An email address has a delimiter between the user portion and domain. If the delimiter is reliable, SPLIT_PART can extract pieces based on structure. This is usually easier to understand than using fixed character positions, which can break when string lengths vary. Parsing converts text into a typed value; formatting converts a typed value into presentation text. Perform analytical work on typed dates and timestamps, then format near the presentation layer. If parsing can fail, validate the incoming pattern first instead of letting one malformed value stop an entire load.

slides.title: SPLIT_PART example
slides.transcript: This query first trims the email and converts it to lowercase. SPLIT_PART then returns the text before or after the at sign. POSITION reports where the delimiter occurs. Run the query and compare the parsed user and domain values. Also notice what happens for missing or malformed email values. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a CRM standardizing names, emails, and phone numbers, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: POSITION answers where
slides.transcript: POSITION returns the location of one substring inside another. It is useful when you need to know whether a delimiter exists or where it occurs. For many parsing tasks, SPLIT_PART is clearer when the delimiter already defines meaningful parts. POSITION is especially useful during inspection and validation. String functions are most useful when the text has a predictable structure. Before extracting a substring, confirm the delimiter or pattern really exists. Regular expressions are powerful, but a complicated regex can become hard to maintain; use the simplest rule that reliably matches the data you actually have.

slides.title: SUBSTRING
slides.transcript: SUBSTRING is useful when character position has a documented meaning. For example, we may take the first three characters of a product name to build a teaching code. But fixed positions can be fragile when string structures vary. Use position-based extraction only when the structure is stable enough to justify it. String functions are most useful when the text has a predictable structure. Before extracting a substring, confirm the delimiter or pattern really exists. Regular expressions are powerful, but a complicated regex can become hard to maintain; use the simplest rule that reliably matches the data you actually have.

slides.title: Create product codes
slides.transcript: This example builds a simple teaching product code. BTRIM cleans the product name. SUBSTRING takes the first three characters. UPPER standardizes the prefix. LPAD pads the numeric ID to three digits. The double-pipe operator concatenates the pieces. The important lesson is that each part of the code comes from a documented transformation. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a CRM standardizing names, emails, and phone numbers, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: REPLACE
slides.transcript: REPLACE is useful for direct literal substitution. If the source system consistently uses a known abbreviation and the business rule says to expand it, REPLACE can be clear and reproducible. But it does not understand context. For flexible patterns, use regular expressions or a lookup table rather than stacking many fragile replacements. String functions are most useful when the text has a predictable structure. Before extracting a substring, confirm the delimiter or pattern really exists. Regular expressions are powerful, but a complicated regex can become hard to maintain; use the simplest rule that reliably matches the data you actually have.

slides.title: REPLACE example
slides.transcript: This example replaces the literal text KB with keyboard. Run the query and compare the raw description with the expanded version. This is appropriate because the transformation rule is explicit and easy to audit. In larger projects, repeated mapping rules may be better stored in reference tables rather than hard-coded into one long SQL expression. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an operations team aligning timestamps across locations, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.transcript: Regular expressions are useful when simple literal functions are not enough. REGEXP_REPLACE can remove or standardize patterns. The tilde operator checks whether a string matches a pattern. Regex is powerful, so keep the rule as simple and explainable as possible. A complicated expression that nobody can review is a data-quality risk of its own. Connect this idea to a CRM standardizing names, emails, and phone numbers. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Regex email cleanup
slides.transcript: This example trims the email, removes characters outside a teaching-level allowed set, and converts the result to lowercase. Run it and compare original and cleaned values. Notice that cleaning a string does not prove the result is valid. Transformation and validation are separate steps. That distinction is important in data preparation. String functions are most useful when the text has a predictable structure. Before extracting a substring, confirm the delimiter or pattern really exists. Regular expressions are powerful, but a complicated regex can become hard to maintain; use the simplest rule that reliably matches the data you actually have.

slides.title: Regex validation
slides.transcript: This query uses a regular expression to check the general shape of an email address. Rows that match are labeled valid shape. Other rows are labeled review. The phrase valid shape is deliberate. A regex can check structure, but it cannot prove that the mailbox exists or that every possible valid internet email syntax is covered. Production validation rules should match the application requirements. String functions are most useful when the text has a predictable structure. Before extracting a substring, confirm the delimiter or pattern really exists. Regular expressions are powerful, but a complicated regex can become hard to maintain; use the simplest rule that reliably matches the data you actually have.

slides.title: Cleaning vs validation
slides.transcript: Cleaning, parsing, validation, and verification are different tasks. Cleaning changes known formatting noise. Parsing extracts meaningful components. Validation checks whether a value follows a rule. Verification asks whether the value corresponds to reality. Keeping these tasks separate makes a preparation pipeline easier to reason about and audit. Text cleaning should separate normalization from interpretation. Trimming spaces or standardizing case is usually safe when the rule is documented; correcting a person's name or guessing an email address is a much stronger intervention. Preserve the original value when auditability matters.

slides.title: Text-function decision guide
slides.transcript: This table summarizes the text half of the module. Use the simplest function that matches the actual problem. Do not use regex when TRIM solves the issue. Do not use fixed positions when a reliable delimiter defines the structure. And do not treat cleaning as proof of validity. Clear, small transformations are easier to maintain and explain. Connect this idea to a hospital calculating length of stay and follow-up dates. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Temporal types
slides.transcript: Now we move from text to temporal data. The first decision is the data type. DATE represents a calendar date. TIMESTAMP represents a date and clock time without time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time. INTERVAL represents a duration. Choosing the correct type is more important than choosing a formatting function. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: DATE
slides.transcript: DATE is appropriate when the calendar day matters but the time of day does not. Examples include birth date or a reporting date. A typed date can be sorted chronologically and used in date arithmetic. A text string that merely looks like a date does not provide the same analytical guarantees. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: TIMESTAMP
slides.transcript: TIMESTAMP stores a date and local clock time. It does not carry a time-zone interpretation. That can be appropriate when the time zone is fixed or irrelevant. But if records come from multiple regions or you need to compare global instants, a plain timestamp can become ambiguous. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: TIMESTAMPTZ
slides.transcript: TIMESTAMPTZ is PostgreSQL's timestamp with time zone type. Conceptually, it represents an instant. PostgreSQL can display that instant in different time zones. This is useful for events collected across locations. The key distinction is between the stored instant and the clock representation shown to a user. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: INTERVAL
slides.transcript: INTERVAL represents duration. You can add an interval to a date or timestamp to create a future or past point. Timestamp subtraction also returns an interval. Intervals are central to PostgreSQL temporal arithmetic and replace many dialect-specific date-add patterns. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: Temporal type decision guide
slides.transcript: Choose the type based on meaning. If only the calendar day matters, DATE may be enough. If you need a local date and time without global time-zone meaning, TIMESTAMP may fit. If the value represents an instant, use TIMESTAMPTZ. If the value is duration, use INTERVAL. Remember that storage precision and analytical grain are separate decisions. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: PostgreSQL date arithmetic
slides.transcript: Here is the PostgreSQL-native approach to common temporal tasks. Subtract timestamps to obtain an interval. Add INTERVAL values to shift time. Use EXTRACT to read components. Use DATE_TRUNC to change analytical grain. Use AGE when you want a symbolic calendar interval. These patterns are clearer and more portable within PostgreSQL than borrowing function names from another SQL dialect. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an operations team aligning timestamps across locations, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: EXTRACT
slides.transcript: EXTRACT reads one component from a date or timestamp. You can extract year, month, day of week, hour, and many other fields. The result is a component value, not a new grouped timestamp. This distinction matters when comparing EXTRACT with DATE_TRUNC. EXTRACT returns a component such as month number or year; DATE_TRUNC returns a timestamp aligned to a time boundary such as the start of the month. For grouping over multiple years, truncating to month is often safer than grouping by month number alone because January 2025 and January 2026 should not be merged accidentally.

slides.title: EXTRACT example
slides.transcript: This query extracts several components from admission timestamps. YEAR and MONTH are straightforward. DOW gives PostgreSQL's numeric day-of-week representation. HOUR gives the clock-hour component. These values are useful as analytical features, but they do not preserve the full timestamp or create a time bucket on their own. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a hospital calculating length of stay and follow-up dates, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Day-of-week caution
slides.transcript: Day-of-week values need documentation. In PostgreSQL, EXTRACT DOW uses zero for Sunday and six for Saturday. Other tools may use different conventions. Whenever a numeric code represents a temporal category, document the mapping before using it in analysis or modeling. Connect this idea to an operations team aligning timestamps across locations. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: DATE_TRUNC
slides.transcript: DATE_TRUNC changes the analytical grain of a timestamp. A timestamp can be truncated to day, week, month, quarter, or other levels. The returned value represents the start of that period. This makes DATE_TRUNC especially useful for GROUP BY because all timestamps in the same period receive the same bucket value. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: DATE_TRUNC example
slides.transcript: Run this query and compare several truncated versions of each order timestamp. The original timestamp keeps the precise event time. The day version maps it to the start of the day. The month version maps it to the start of the month. This is how a precise event can be analyzed at a coarser reporting grain without changing the stored source value. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a hospital calculating length of stay and follow-up dates, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: EXTRACT vs DATE_TRUNC
slides.transcript: EXTRACT and DATE_TRUNC solve different problems. EXTRACT month gives a number such as three. DATE_TRUNC month gives a full month bucket such as March first, twenty twenty-six at midnight. If you group only by month number, March from multiple years can be combined accidentally. DATE_TRUNC often gives a safer full-period key for time-series aggregation. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: Monthly aggregation
slides.transcript: This query truncates each order timestamp to month grain. It then groups orders by that month bucket. COUNT measures order volume, and SUM calculates monthly revenue. The cast to date is mainly for a simpler displayed month label. The important analytical decision is the month-level grain created by DATE_TRUNC. EXTRACT returns a component such as month number or year; DATE_TRUNC returns a timestamp aligned to a time boundary such as the start of the month. For grouping over multiple years, truncating to month is often safer than grouping by month number alone because January 2025 and January 2026 should not be merged accidentally.

slides.title: Monthly revenue visual
slides.transcript: This visual shows the effect of changing grain. The source table has one row per order. After DATE_TRUNC and GROUP BY, the result has one row per month. The chart is not just a different display. It represents a different analytical grain. Always be clear about what one row means before and after aggregation. EXTRACT returns a component such as month number or year; DATE_TRUNC returns a timestamp aligned to a time boundary such as the start of the month. For grouping over multiple years, truncating to month is often safer than grouping by month number alone because January 2025 and January 2026 should not be merged accidentally.

slides.title: Timestamp subtraction
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL can subtract one timestamp from another. The result is an INTERVAL representing elapsed time. This is the direct way to answer questions such as length of stay or processing duration. If you later need a numeric number of hours or days, that is a separate conversion step. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: Length of stay
slides.transcript: This query first subtracts admit time from discharge time. That produces an interval. It also converts the interval to seconds using EXTRACT EPOCH, divides by the number of seconds in a day, and rounds the result. The interval is a typed duration. The numeric day value is an analytical representation derived from that duration. Text cleaning should separate normalization from interpretation. Trimming spaces or standardizing case is usually safe when the rule is documented; correcting a person's name or guessing an email address is a much stronger intervention. Preserve the original value when auditability matters.

slides.title: EPOCH conversion
slides.transcript: EXTRACT EPOCH returns the total number of seconds represented by an interval. From there, you can convert to hours or days. The unit you choose should match the analysis. A numeric duration is often convenient for statistics or modeling, while the interval type can be more expressive for SQL temporal operations. Date arithmetic should reflect the business definition. Calendar age, elapsed hours, and number of midnights are not always the same measure. In healthcare, length of stay may have an operational definition that differs from simple timestamp subtraction. Document the unit and the rule.

slides.title: Adding intervals
slides.transcript: Intervals can also shift time. Adding fourteen days to a discharge timestamp creates a follow-up point two weeks later. Adding thirty days creates a longer window. The interval makes the rule explicit and readable in PostgreSQL. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: Follow-up dates
slides.transcript: This query creates two follow-up timestamps. The original discharge time remains visible. Then PostgreSQL adds fourteen-day and thirty-day intervals. Keeping the original and derived times side by side makes the transformation easy to audit and explain. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: AGE vs subtraction
slides.transcript: AGE and direct subtraction both compare two temporal values, but their emphasis differs. AGE expresses a symbolic calendar interval using years, months, and days. Direct subtraction gives the elapsed interval between two timestamps. For hospital length of stay, direct subtraction is usually easier to interpret. For calendar-style age differences, AGE may be more natural. Date arithmetic should reflect the business definition. Calendar age, elapsed hours, and number of midnights are not always the same measure. In healthcare, length of stay may have an operational definition that differs from simple timestamp subtraction. Document the unit and the rule.

slides.title: Parsing vs formatting
slides.transcript: Parsing and formatting move in opposite directions. Parsing starts with text and creates a typed date or timestamp. That typed value can be sorted, compared, grouped, and used in arithmetic. Formatting starts with a typed temporal value and creates text for human presentation. For analytics, parse early and format late. Parsing converts text into a typed value; formatting converts a typed value into presentation text. Perform analytical work on typed dates and timestamps, then format near the presentation layer. If parsing can fail, validate the incoming pattern first instead of letting one malformed value stop an entire load.

slides.title: Casting vs parsing
slides.transcript: Sometimes a direct cast is sufficient. If the text is already in a clear date format that PostgreSQL recognizes and you have validated the input, casting to date can be simple. When the format is different, TO_DATE lets you specify the pattern. For mixed raw input, first identify the shape and then apply the appropriate parser. Blindly parsing unknown text can cause errors or incorrect interpretations. Parsing converts text into a typed value; formatting converts a typed value into presentation text. Perform analytical work on typed dates and timestamps, then format near the presentation layer. If parsing can fail, validate the incoming pattern first instead of letting one malformed value stop an entire load.

slides.title: Safe parsing workflow
slides.transcript: A safe parsing workflow starts by cleaning boundary whitespace. Then identify the input shape. Apply the parser that matches that shape. If the value does not match an expected format, return NULL or flag it for review instead of guessing. Parsing converts representation. It does not prove that the underlying business value is accurate. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an operations team aligning timestamps across locations, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Safe date parsing
slides.transcript: This query uses CASE to handle several known date formats. Blank strings become NULL. ISO-style text can be cast to date. Slash-formatted text uses TO_DATE with a month-day-year pattern. Eight-digit text uses a year-month-day pattern. Anything else becomes NULL for review. The important idea is explicit, controlled parsing rather than guessing. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: TO_CHAR
slides.transcript: TO_CHAR converts a typed date or timestamp into formatted text. This is useful for reports, labels, exports, and human-facing displays. But once you turn a timestamp into arbitrary text, temporal sorting and arithmetic become less direct. Keep the value typed through analytical processing and format it near the reporting boundary. Parsing converts text into a typed value; formatting converts a typed value into presentation text. Perform analytical work on typed dates and timestamps, then format near the presentation layer. If parsing can fail, validate the incoming pattern first instead of letting one malformed value stop an entire load.

slides.title: Why formatting comes late
slides.transcript: Typed timestamps are more useful for analysis than display strings. They sort chronologically, support arithmetic, and retain temporal semantics. A formatted string is useful for a person but less flexible for computation. That is why formatting generally belongs near the output boundary rather than early in the preparation pipeline. Parsing converts text into a typed value; formatting converts a typed value into presentation text. Perform analytical work on typed dates and timestamps, then format near the presentation layer. If parsing can fail, validate the incoming pattern first instead of letting one malformed value stop an entire load.

slides.title: Time zones
slides.transcript: Time zones are easier when you separate the instant from its display. A timestamptz represents an instant. That instant can be displayed using Eastern time, UTC, or another zone. The clock reading changes, but the underlying instant does not. This distinction is essential for logs, orders, and events collected across locations. Time zones matter whenever events from different locations need to be compared on one timeline. Store instants in a consistent form, often using TIMESTAMPTZ, and convert to local time for presentation. Do not permanently rewrite an instant just because a report needs to display it in a local zone.

slides.title: Timestamp vs timestamptz
slides.transcript: A plain timestamp stores a local date and time without time-zone interpretation. A timestamptz represents an instant. If data crosses regions, plain local timestamps can become ambiguous. When the same event must be understood consistently across systems, timestamptz is usually the safer model. Choose temporal types based on meaning. DATE is for calendar dates without time of day. TIMESTAMP stores a date and time without a time-zone interpretation. TIMESTAMPTZ represents an instant in time and is usually safer for events that cross regions or daylight-saving changes.

slides.title: AT TIME ZONE
slides.transcript: This query displays order timestamps using two time zones. AT TIME ZONE America slash New York gives an Eastern local clock representation. AT TIME ZONE UTC gives a UTC clock representation. Run the query and compare the displayed times. The underlying event instant is the same; only the clock representation changes. Time zones matter whenever events from different locations need to be compared on one timeline. Store instants in a consistent form, often using TIMESTAMPTZ, and convert to local time for presentation. Do not permanently rewrite an instant just because a report needs to display it in a local zone.
